name: Hide Artifacts
description:
Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection. Operating systems may have features to hide various artifacts, such as important system files and administrative task execution, to avoid disrupting user work environments and prevent users from changing files or features on the system. Adversaries may abuse these features to hide artifacts such as files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity to evade detection.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit)(Citation: MalwareBytes ADS July 2015)

Adversaries may also attempt to hide artifacts associated with malicious behavior by creating computing regions that are isolated from common security instrumentation, such as through the use of virtualization technology.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)

references.description: Amit Serper. (2016). Cybereason Lab Analysis OSX.Pirrit. Retrieved December 10, 2021.
Arntz, P. (2015, July 22). Introduction to Alternate Data Streams. Retrieved March 21, 2018.
Dani Creus, Tyler Halfpop, Robert Falcone. (2016, September 26). Sofacy's 'Komplex' OS X Trojan. Retrieved July 8, 2017.
SophosLabs. (2020, May 21). Ragnar Locker ransomware deploys virtual machine to dodge security. Retrieved June 29, 2020.

telemetry.name: Application Log Content
telemetry.description: Application-emitted audit or operational event content.
telemetry.collection_focus: Select the application event family required by the detection and document its native schema before normalization.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

telemetry.name: Command Execution
telemetry.description: Execution of a command and its interpreter or parent context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect process command lines and relevant shell/interpreter audit; shell history alone is neither complete nor tamper-resistant.

providers.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
providers.scope: Script content via event 4104 when configured; channel depends on PowerShell edition.

providers.name: Sysmon process events
providers.scope: Interpreter launch and parent context, not full script content.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: execve-family execution context; shell built-ins need additional instrumentation.

configuration: Enable Script Block Logging through the policy/configuration for the installed edition. Forward Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for Windows PowerShell, or PowerShellCore/Operational for PowerShell 7.
Retain script-block ID and fragment ordering alongside process creation. Protect access to collected script text; secrets may be included.
On Linux, use narrowly scoped Audit execution rules for the lab account and supported architectures, and retain joined SYSCALL/EXECVE/PATH records.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Script content and process command lines are different signals. Logging may be partial, fragmented, filtered or disabled; never assume a command line reveals everything executed.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and principal: rare interpreters, command argument patterns and parent-child sequences. Normalize scripts carefully; obfuscation, administrative automation and missing command lines change visibility.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.name: Apple Endpoint Security clients
providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.

telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

telemetry.name: File Metadata
telemetry.description: File attributes such as path, size, timestamps, ownership and cryptographic hash.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect scoped file inventory/FIM metadata with hash algorithm and observation time; preserve original timestamps separately from collector time.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.description: Creation of a process with executable, command line, parent and security context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect Sysmon ProcessCreate (1); preserve ProcessGuid and parent identifiers. Security 4688 is an alternative with separate audit/command-line settings.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hidden Artifacts Across Platforms

analytics.name: Analytic 1384
analytics.guidance: Abuse of file/registry attributes to hide malicious files, directories, or services. Defender view: detection of attrib.exe setting hidden/system flags, creation of Alternate Data Streams, or registry keys altering file visibility.

tuning.description: Filter for sensitive file types likely targeted for hiding.
Enable or disable detection of Alternate Data Streams depending on business use.

analytics.name: Analytic 1385
analytics.guidance: Hidden file creation using leading '.' or file attribute changes with chattr (immutable/hidden flags). Defender view: detect execution of chattr, lsattr anomalies, and unusual hidden files appearing in system directories.

tuning.description: Restrict hidden file detection to privileged system directories.
Tune for specific chattr flags (+i immutable, +a append-only) most abused for persistence.

log_sources.name: auditd:EXECVE
log_sources.channel: Execution of chattr to set +i or +a attributes

log_sources.name: auditd:FILE
log_sources.channel: Creation of hidden files (.*) in sensitive directories (/etc, /var, /usr/bin)

analytics.name: Analytic 1386
analytics.guidance: Hidden files via 'chflags hidden' or Apple-specific attributes, LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons placed in non-standard hidden directories. Defender view: detect command execution modifying file flags and unusual plist creation in hidden paths.

tuning.description: List of directories monitored for hidden plist or agent placement.

log_sources.name: macos:unifiedlog
log_sources.channel: Execution of chflags hidden or setfile -a V

log_sources.name: macos:unifiedlog
log_sources.channel: Creation of LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons in hidden or non-standard directories

analytics.name: Analytic 1387
analytics.guidance: Abuse of VMFS or ESXi shell to hide datastore files, renaming/moving VMDK or VMX files into hidden directories. Defender view: anomalous ESXi shell commands or file operations obscuring VM artifacts.

tuning.description: Restrict to VMDK, VMX, or log files critical for VM operations.

log_sources.name: esxi:shell
log_sources.channel: mv, rename, or chmod commands moving VM files into hidden directories

log_sources.name: esxi:syslog
log_sources.channel: Datastore file hidden or renamed unexpectedly

analytics.name: Analytic 1388
analytics.guidance: Malicious macros or embedded objects hidden within Office documents by renaming streams or using hidden OLE objects. Defender view: detection of hidden macro streams or objects in documents correlated with anomalous execution.

tuning.description: Tune detection to specific Office apps and document types where macros are disallowed.

log_sources.name: m365:unified
log_sources.channel: Detection of hidden macro streams or SetHiddenAttribute actions

software.name: Remcos
software.description: [Remcos](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0332) can modify file attributes to hide the file.(Citation: Fortinet Remcos Campaign NOV 2024)

references.description: Zhang, X. (2024, November 8). New Campaign Uses Remcos RAT to Exploit Victims. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

software.name: OSX/Shlayer
software.description: [OSX/Shlayer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0402) has used the mktemp utility to make random and unique filenames for payloads, such as export tmpDir="$(mktemp -d /tmp/XXXXXXXXXXXX)" or mktemp -t Installer.(Citation: sentinelone shlayer to zshlayer)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)(Citation: Shlayer jamf gatekeeper bypass 2021)

references.description: Jaron Bradley. (2021, April 26). Shlayer malware abusing Gatekeeper bypass on macOS. Retrieved September 22, 2021.
Phil Stokes. (2020, September 8). Coming Out of Your Shell: From Shlayer to ZShlayer. Retrieved September 13, 2021.
Phil Stokes. (2021, February 16). 20 Common Tools & Techniques Used by macOS Threat Actors & Malware. Retrieved August 23, 2021.

software.name: Bundlore
software.description: [Bundlore](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0482) uses the mktemp utility to make unique file and directory names for payloads, such as TMP_DIR=`mktemp -d -t x.(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

references.description: Phil Stokes. (2021, February 16). 20 Common Tools & Techniques Used by macOS Threat Actors & Malware. Retrieved August 23, 2021.

software.name: WarzoneRAT
software.description: [WarzoneRAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0670) can masquerade the Process Environment Block on a compromised host to hide its attempts to elevate privileges through `IFileOperation`.(Citation: Check Point Warzone Feb 2020)

references.description: Harakhavik, Y. (2020, February 3). Warzone: Behind the enemy lines. Retrieved December 17, 2021.

software.name: Tarrask
software.description: [Tarrask](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1011) is able to create “hidden” scheduled tasks by deleting the Security Descriptor (`SD`) registry value.(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task)

references.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Team & Detection and Response Team . (2022, April 12). Tarrask malware uses scheduled tasks for defense evasion. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

software.name: DarkTortilla
software.description: [DarkTortilla](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1066) has used `%HiddenReg%` and `%HiddenKey%` as part of its persistence via the Windows registry.(Citation: Secureworks DarkTortilla Aug 2022)

references.description: Secureworks Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2022, August 17). DarkTortilla Malware Analysis. Retrieved November 3, 2022.

software.name: NOOPLDR
software.description: [NOOPLDR](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S9025) can hide services used to aid execution.(Citation: JPCERT MirrorFace JUL 2024)

references.description: Tomonaga, S. (2024, July 16). MirrorFace Attack against Japanese Organisations. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

mitigations.name: Application Developer Guidance
mitigations.description: Application developers should consider limiting the requirements for custom or otherwise difficult to manage file/folder exclusions. Where possible, install applications to trusted system folder paths that are already protected by restricted file and directory permissions.

mitigations.name: Limit Software Installation
mitigations.description: Restrict the installation of software that may be abused to create hidden desktops, such as hVNC, to user groups that require it.

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.description: Periodically audit virtual machines for abnormalities.

mitigations.name: Antivirus/Antimalware
mitigations.description: Review and audit file/folder exclusions, and limit scope of exclusions to only what is required where possible.(Citation: Microsoft File Folder Exclusions)

references.description: Microsoft. (2024, February 27). Contextual file and folder exclusions. Retrieved March 29, 2024.

candidates.name: Extract binary files via VBA
candidates.description:
This module extracts a binary (calc.exe) from inside of another binary. 

In the wild maldoc authors will use this technique to hide binaries inside of files stored 
within the office document itself. An example of this technique can be seen in sample

f986040c7dd75b012e7dfd876acb33a158abf651033563ab068800f07f508226

This sample contains a document inside of itself. Document 1 is the actual maldoc itself, document 2
is the same document without all the malicious code. Document 1 will copy Document 2 to the file system
and then "peek" inside of this document and pull out the oleObject.bin file. Contained inside of this
oleObject.bin file is a payload that is parsed out and executed on the file system.

simulation.prerequisites: Use disposable lab hosts and test accounts, explicit target allowlists, a clean snapshot, bounded egress and a restore plan. Review every candidate and dependency before any execution.

synthetic.purpose: Collection/parser contract exercise, NOT a positive example or detection of this TTP.
